textbookText: Class 6: Cephalopoda (Gr; kephale-head; podos-foot) i. They are extremely found in marine water. ii. Body is elongated and bilaterally symmetrical and divisible into head and trunk. iii. Shell is external, internal or absent. iv. Head bears eyes, mouth, tentacles and radula. v. Suckers are found in arms or tentacles encircling mouth. vi. Sexes are separate.
Example: Sepia (cuttle fish), Loligo (squid), Octopus (devil fish), Nautilus etc. 8.2.9 PHYLUM ECHINODERMATA (Gr; echinos-hedgehog or spiny, derma-skin)

The term echinodermata literally means spiny skinned and was first introduced by klein in 1734 for “sea urchins”. Because of their radial symmetry, they were kept with coelenterates in a single group ‘radiata’ for a long time. Later, they were recognized as distinct group by leukart in 1847. All the animals of phylum echinodermata form a peculiar group of invertebrates, living at the bottom of sea by creeping slowly, though some can swim.

General characters 1. They are exclusively found in marine water, mostly in sea bottom and hence called ‘benthic invertebrates. 2. The shape of the body varies among the species, which are cylindrical or elongated, globular, star like, discoidal, or flower like. 3. They are triploblastic and have organ grade of body organization. 4. Adults have pentamerous radially symmetrical body and larvae are bilaterally symmetrical. 5. They are enterocoelomate animals. 6. They have no definite head. Body surface is divided into oral and aboral surface where oral surface is marked by five symmetrically radiating areas called ambulacra and five alternating interambulacra. 7. Body wall consists of outermost epidermis, dermis, muscular layer and innermost epithelial layer (ciliated cuboidal). 8. Many of them bear pincer like pedicellaria with spine on body surface; pedicellaria clear body by removing debris and other things which are attached on the body.

9. Endoskeleton consists of calcareous ossicles or plates of mesodermal origin in dermis. 10. Water vascular system or ambulacral system of coelomic origin, consisting of canals

filled with water-like fluid connected with tube feet and madreporite. 11. Tube feet are the locomotory organ which consists of ampulla, podium and sucker. 12. Alimentary canal is either straight or coiled and mouth is present on the oral surface and anus usually on the aboral surface. 13. Circulatory system is open type which includes haemal and perihaemal systems with sinuses but without heart. A true blood vascular system is lacking. 14. Excretory system is entirely absent. However, nitrogenous wastes are expelled out by papulae and tube feet in some forms. 15. Nervous system is primitive or poorly developed with a circum-oral ring and radial nerves. Brain is absent. 16. Sexes are separate with few exceptions. Reproduction occurs both sexually and asexually. Asexual reproduction takes place by regeneration. 17. Fertilization is external. Development is indirect with larval forms. 18. Larvae are free swimming and bilaterally symmetrical, get metamorphosed into radially symmetrical adult. Some echinoderms are viviparous.

Unique features All marine animals, skin with calcareous spine, enterocoelomate, presence of water vascular system, some with pincer like pedicellaria on body surface, locomotion by tube feet, excretory system lacking, absence of brain and heart, larva bilaterally symmetrical but adult radially symmetrical, well-marked regeneration power Classification Phylum echinodermata is divided into two subphyla: Eleutherozoa and Pelmatozoa Subphylum: Eleutherozoa (eleutheros-free; zoon-animal): They are free living forms and further divided into four classes on the basis of body shape:

Class 1: Asteroidea i. They are commonly called starfishes or sea star. ii. They have five arms, not distinct from central disc. iii. Presence of tube feet with suckers, and pedicellaria. iv. Their larvae are called bipinnaria and brachiolaria.
Example: Asterias (sea star), Solaster etc.

Class 2: Ophiuroidea (Gr; ophis-snake; oura-tail; eidos-form) i. They are commonly called brittle star. ii. Their body is also star like but arms are sharply marked off from the central disc. iii. Pedicellaria is absent, tube feet without suckers. iv. Larva is called ophiopluteus.
Example: Ophioderma, Ophiura etc. Class: 3 Echinoidea (Gr; echinos- hedgehog; eidos-form) i. They are commonly called sea urchins.

ii. Body is discoidal, or oval and without arms iii. Pedicellaria are present and 3-jawed. iv. Their biting and chewing apparatus is called ‘Aristotle lantern’. v. Larva is called echinopluteus.
Example: Echinus (sea urchin), Echinocardium (heart urchin), Clypeaster (sand dollar)
